Drawing on biographer Paul Williams's characterization of Dick as a 'reluctant convention-goer' and the introduction to The Last Interview and Other Conversations, the document establishes that Dick's public presence was concentrated primarily between 1972 and 1982, with very little documented activity during his most prolific publishing period of the 1960s. page_summary: This research document provides a systematic audit of the full scope of Philip K. Dick's documented public appearances across his life and career. Drawing on biographer Paul Williams's characterization of Dick as a 'reluctant convention-goer' and the introduction to The Last Interview and Other Conversations, the document establishes that Dick's public presence was concentrated primarily between 1972 and 1982, with virtually no documented activity during the 1960s when he published most of his major works. The audit begins with Dick's first major public lecture on February 17, 1972, 'The Android and the Human,' delivered at a luncheon at the University of British Columbia's Faculty Club in Vancouver, introduced by Professor Susan Wood's English department. Dick repeated this keynote the following day at VCON 2 at the Biltmore Hotel in Vancouver, where fewer than 100 people attended and Dick made headlines by announcing he intended to remain in Canada. The document covers the July 18, 1973 recorded talk at Cal State Fullerton with Professor Willis E. McNelly, who had persuaded Dick to donate his manuscripts to CSUF's Special Collections Library. Dick's appearance as Professional Guest of Honor at Westercon 27 in Santa Barbara (July 3-7, 1974) is noted. The most extensively documented appearance is Dick's September 24, 1977 speech at the Second International Science Fiction Festival in Metz, France, where he delivered 'If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others,' declaring that 'we are living in a computer-programmed reality.' The audit records that the speech was poorly received, with Dick speaking in monotone and the interpreter's transcript differing from his actual words due to a last-minute rewrite. The document also covers 'How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later' (1978), noting it was written in speech form but never actually delivered as a lecture. Multiple radio appearances in Vancouver and Los Angeles are catalogued, as are interviews conducted at the Metz festival by Uwe Anton, Werner Fuchs, Yves Breux, and Francis Luxereau.

## Comprehensive Audit of Philip K. Dick's Public Appearances and Speeches 

## Overview 

Philip K. Dick (1928–1982) was famously reclusive. Biographer Paul Williams described him as a "reluctant convention-goer," and the introduction to The Last Interview and Other Conversations notes that "nearly all the interviews that exist were done in the last decade of his life" and that "in the 1960s, when he published most of his major works, there was essentially nothing". Dick's public appearances were rare, concentrated primarily between 1972 and 1982, and constitute a surprisingly small body of documented events for one of the 20th century's most in�uential science �ction writers.[1][2] 

## Major Speeches and Lectures 

## 1. "The Android and the Human" — UBC Faculty Luncheon Lecture (February 17, 1972) 

On February 17, 1972, Dick gave his �rst major public lecture at a luncheon held in his honor at the University of British Columbia's Faculty Club in Vancouver. Introduced by Professor Susan Wood's English department, Dick spoke to a "large, �lled lecture hall" and the speech was "very well received". The talk examined how modern technology creates an illusion of animation in machines, arguing that rather than studying machines to understand humans, scientists should study humans to understand machine behavior.[3][4][5][6] 

## 2. "The Android and the Human" — VCON 2 Keynote (February 18–19, 1972) 

The following day, Dick repeated his "Android and the Human" speech as his keynote address at VCON 2, the Second Annual Vancouver Science Fiction Convention, held at the Biltmore Hotel in Vancouver. Fewer than 100 people attended the convention, where Dick served as Guest of Honor with Mike Horvat as Toastmaster. Dick was energetic and sociable, mingling enthusiastically with fans and making headlines in the Vancouver Province when he announced he intended to remain in Canada. The speech was subsequently published in SF Commentary, issue 31.[5][7][3] 

## 3. Talk at California State University, Fullerton (July 18, 1973) 

On July 18, 1973, Dick gave a recorded talk at Cal State Fullerton with Dr. White and Professor Willis E. McNelly. McNelly, who had initiated a correspondence with Dick during his stay at the X-Kalay recovery program in Vancouver, had persuaded Dick to donate his manuscripts to CSUF's Special Collections Library. The talk covered issues in science �ction writing, the role of science �ction in society, and included an audience Q&A session.[8][9][10] 

## 4. Westercon 27 — Guest of Honor (July 3–7, 1974, Santa Barbara, CA) 

Dick served as Professional Guest of Honor at Westercon 27, held July 3–7, 1974, at the Francisco Torres in Santa Barbara, California. Fan Guest of Honor was Charles Burbee. This was a notable public appearance for Dick, though detailed records of any speci�c speech he delivered at this convention are sparse in the available documentation.[11][12]
